steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on customizing neural machine translation models for individual users' style and domain needs with pluggable, memory-augmented adapters. Motivate the problem, discuss plugin-based approaches and their limits, and summarize our method and its challenges.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Background: NMT trained on large general web data
2. Problem: customers need style- and domain-specific customization
3. Pluggable methods as a solution
4. Limits of parametric plugins; idea of memory-augmented adapter
5. Challenges and our approach (memories, adapter, training), experiments

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Background
- modern NMT systems built on large-scale parallel data from the Web
- style/content follow average distribution over many domains
- strong NMT close to or better than human translators in general domain

2. Customer requirements
- special style- and domain-specific individual demands
- e.g. translations in a special style; medical texts
- diverse across customers; retraining/fine-tuning per user is costly, esp. with limited user data

3. Pluggable methods
- additional modules steer pretrained models
- Figure 1: users give text samples for NMT model to imitate
- learn plugin to control NMT model, original parameters untouched
- keeps pretrained performance, alleviates catastrophic forgetting

4. Parametric plugins and their bottleneck
- lightweight parametric plugins for controlling pretrained models; for MT can tailor behavior to diverse demands
- performance bottleneck of fully-parametric pluggable methods: more trainable parameters not always better
- inspired by retrieval-augmented models -> increase expressive power of parametric plugins through external memories = memory-augmented adapter

5. Challenges and method
- two challenges: (1) memories with useful customization info; (2) integrating memories into NMT models without quality loss
- long phrases: more context but harder to match than short ones
- multi-granular memories: balance context vs retrieval difficulty
- unlike previous works (key = source sentence + target prefix, value = next token), multi-scale translation knowledge, suits queries from different layers
- new adapter architecture to interpolate original representation and retrieved vectors
- training strategy with memory dropout -> fewer spurious dependencies on memory
- experiments: style- and domain-related customization; better than many representative baselines

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recently, modern neural machine translation (NMT) systems are often built with large-scale parallel data that is extracted from the Web, and the style and content of this data are driven by the average distribution of data from many domains. So the performance of strong NMT models is close to human translators or even better than them in the general domain.

But MT customers may have special requirements, which include individual demands that are specific to a style or a domain. For example, some users may want translations in a special style, and some others may need to translate medical texts. These requirements can be very different from customer to customer, and retraining or fine-tuning the model for each user costs a lot of development effort, especially when the users only have limited data.

Pluggable methods give hope for handling these user requirements. They use additional modules to steer pretrained models. As shown in Figure 1, users can give some text samples for the NMT model to imitate. We then learn a plugin that controls the NMT model so that it satisfies the user demands, without optimizing the parameters of the original model. This way we keep the performance of the pretrained model and reduce the risk of catastrophic forgetting.

4. Parametric plugins and their bottleneck
- lightweight parametric plugins for controlling pretrained models; for MT can tailor behavior to diverse demands
- performance bottleneck of fully-parametric pluggable methods: more trainable parameters not always better
- inspired by retrieval-augmented models -> increase expressive power of parametric plugins through external memories = memory-augmented adapter

5. Challenges and method
- two challenges: (1) memories with useful customization info; (2) integrating memories into NMT models without quality loss
- long phrases: more context but harder to match than short ones
- multi-granular memories: balance context vs retrieval difficulty
- unlike previous works (key = source sentence + target prefix, value = next token), multi-scale translation knowledge, suits queries from different layers
- new adapter architecture to interpolate original representation and retrieved vectors
- training strategy with memory dropout -> fewer spurious dependencies on memory
- experiments: style- and domain-related customization; better than many representative baselines

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recently, modern neural machine translation (NMT) systems are often built with large-scale parallel data that is extracted from the Web, and the style and content of this data are driven by the average distribution of data from many domains. So the performance of strong NMT models is close to human translators or even better than them in the general domain.

But MT customers may have special requirements, which include individual demands that are specific to a style or a domain. For example, some users may want translations in a special style, and some others may need to translate medical texts. These requirements can be very different from customer to customer, and retraining or fine-tuning the model for each user costs a lot of development effort, especially when the users only have limited data.

Pluggable methods give hope for handling these user requirements. They use additional modules to steer pretrained models. As shown in Figure 1, users can give some text samples for the NMT model to imitate. We then learn a plugin that controls the NMT model so that it satisfies the user demands, without optimizing the parameters of the original model. This way we keep the performance of the pretrained model and reduce the risk of catastrophic forgetting.

Some researchers propose lightweight parametric plugins for controlling pretrained models. In machine translation, plugins like these can also tailor the behavior of the model to diverse user demands. But recent studies find that fully-parametric pluggable methods have a performance bottleneck, because adding more trainable parameters does not always give better performance. We are inspired by recent progress in retrieval-augmented models, and we propose to increase the expressive power of parametric plugins by using external memories. We call this a memory-augmented adapter.

There are two main challenges for the memory-augmented adapter: (1) how to construct memories that provide useful customization information, and (2) how to integrate the memories into existing NMT models without losing quality. Long phrases give more contextualized information, but it is harder to match long sequences between queries and memory items than to match short ones. So we propose to build multi-granular memories, which balance the amount of contextualized information and the difficulty of retrieval. Many previous works encode the source sentence and the target prefix as the key and the next token as the value. Our memory is different: it provides multi-scale translation knowledge that suits queries from different layers of the NMT model. For integrating the memory, we propose a new adapter architecture that interpolates the original model representation and the retrieved vectors better. We also propose a new training strategy with memory dropout, which reduces spurious dependencies between the NMT model and the given memory. We run experiments on both style-related and domain-related customization, and the results show that our method is better than many representative baselines.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In recent years, modern neural machine translation (NMT; [1]) systems are often developed with large-scale parallel data extracted from the Web [2,3], whose style and content are driven by the average distribution of data from many domains [4]. As a result, the performance of strong NMT models is close to or even better than that of human translators in the general domain [5,6].

However, MT customers may have special requirements, including style- and domain-specific individual demands [7,8]. For instance, some users may want translations in a special style, while others may need to translate medical texts. These requirements can be quite diverse among customers, and retraining or fine-tuning the model for each user entails significant development costs, especially with limited user data.

Fortunately, pluggable methods [9,10,11], which employ additional modules to steer pretrained models, bring hope for handling these user requirements. As shown in Figure 1, users can provide some text samples for the NMT model to imitate. We then learn a plugin that controls the NMT model to satisfy the user demands without optimizing the parameters of the original model, so that we maintain the performance of the pretrained model and alleviate the risk of catastrophic forgetting [12].

Some researchers suggest lightweight parametric plugins for controlling pretrained models [13,14,15,16,17,18], and for machine translation such plugins can also tailor model behavior to diverse user demands. However, recent studies find a performance bottleneck in fully-parametric pluggable methods [14,17,19]: increasing the number of trainable parameters does not always lead to better performance. Inspired by the recent progress of retrieval-augmented models [20,21,22,11,23], we propose to increase the expressive power [17] of parametric plugins through external memories, which we term a memory-augmented adapter.

The main challenges of the memory-augmented adapter are two-fold: (1) constructing memories that provide useful customization information; and (2) integrating the memories into existing NMT models without quality loss. Although long phrases provide more contextualized information, matching long sequences between queries and memory items is more difficult than matching shorter ones. We therefore build multi-granular memories to balance the amount of contextualized information and the retrieval difficulty. Unlike many previous works [21,22,11] that encode the source sentence and target prefix as the key and the next token as the value, our memory provides multi-scale translation knowledge [24] suitable for queries coming from different layers of the NMT model [25]. For memory integration, we propose a new adapter architecture that better interpolates the original model representation and the retrieved vectors. Moreover, we propose a training strategy with memory dropout to reduce spurious dependencies between the NMT model and the provided memory. Experiments on both style- and domain-related customizations show the superiority of our method over many representative baselines.
